Historical Background: The source describes a small brick temple of Shri Kalika Devi that existed in a forest at the southern end of Nashik from ancient times of the Maratha kingdom. The Navratri Yatra began at Sri Kalika Mandir, and pilgrims and devotees gradually started gathering there. After independence, pilgrims from religious events began visiting the temple, and the annual pilgrimage developed.
Rituals: Darshan and pilgrimage
Fair Activities: Pilgrimage, darshan, and social welfare activities
Cultural Significance: The yatra is associated with the long-standing Kalika Devi temple tradition in Nashik. The temple trust also conducts charitable activities, including donations and support for schools, orphanages, hospitals, earthquake victims, and other welfare initiatives.

Historical Background: Annual celebration associated with Nashik's grape harvest and wine-producing region
Rituals: Grape harvest activities and farmer showcase
Fair Activities: Grape stalls, farmers' market, cooking competition, winery tours, folk dance, art workshops
Cultural Significance: Promotes Nashik's agricultural and grape-growing heritage

Historical Background: Maharashtra Tourism event combining nature, adventure and cultural experiences
Rituals: Rural/cultural experiences; workshops
Fair Activities: Trekking, cycling, paragliding, ATV rides, craft & food bazaar, cultural activities
Cultural Significance: Tourism-oriented cultural and adventure event in the Nashik region

Historical Background: Traditional Pawara community celebration associated with the period preceding Holi.
Rituals: Community gathers at a common place; people exchange greetings; gulal is smeared on foreheads/cheeks. Young men and women traditionally use the occasion to propose marriage.
Fair Activities: Community gathering and social interaction
Cultural Significance: Provides a traditional social and cultural setting, including partner selection and community interaction

Deity: Gods and goddesses; specific deity not named
Historical Background: Traditional Pawara celebration occurring before the main Holi festival.
Rituals: Community gathers at a nearby weekly bazaar; rally with dhol; Gav Patil is invited for worship of gods and goddesses; musical instrument, dancing and singing competitions.
Fair Activities: Dhol, musical competitions, dancing, singing and rally
Cultural Significance: Demonstrates Pawara tribal culture, music, dance and collective celebration

Duration: Preparations begin about one month in advance
Historical Background: Sacred bamboo Danda is brought from the forest with puja and offerings; Holi stick is erected; bonfire is lit; singing and dancing take place
Rituals: Coconut, sugar bangles
Fair Activities: N/A
Cultural Significance: IndiaDistricts – Dhule Festivals & Fairs

Duration: Originated centuries ago as a harvest celebration, trading event and occasion for marriage arrangements
Historical Background: Colored powder is applied by young men and women to express marriage interest; village-head rally and traditional performances take place
Rituals: N/A
Fair Activities: massive tribal folk dances to the beat of giant dhol drums, the Gol Gadhedo greased-pole climbing competition, and vibrant market trading for Holi essentials
Cultural Significance: it is a celebration of tribal identity, gender equality, and agricultural prosperity. Observed primarily by the Bhil and Bhilala communities

Duration: Five consecutive years required for fulfilling the vow
Historical Background: Associated with the traditional story of Kumbadanu, Burmavajan and Indi Raja and the granting of mannat
Rituals: Puja, bhajan, music, dancing, folk songs and dramatic performances depicting the history of Indi Raja; bhandara
Fair Activities: Social gathering, folk dance, music and natak performances
Cultural Significance: Fulfills vows and preserves Pawara oral history, folk traditions and community gathering

Duration: Five days; fifth day is Pachavi
Historical Background: Phag means donation/subscription; traditionally associated with the period following Holi
Rituals: Budla performers move through villages collecting donations; villagers and children dress in costumes; Pavvi observers traditionally follow dietary practices; fifth-day community meal
Fair Activities: Singing, comedy, drama, dance, costumes and playful performances
Cultural Significance: Preserves community arts, folk performances, collective meals and traditional donation practices

Historical Background: Observed for more than 195 years in connection with the punyatithi of Samarth Khandoji Maharaj
Rituals: Puja at Shree Vitthal Mandir; devotees also worship Rukhmini Mata; traditional soang performances are presented
Fair Activities: Soang performances depicting Shiv-Parvati, Rakshas Vadh and Ramayan
Cultural Significance: Maintains a long-standing religious and theatrical folk tradition centered on the temple and jatra

Historical Background: Began nearly 168 years ago; associated with eight devotees including Vallab Kashiram Tambad, Hemlal Gujarati and Keshav Deshpande; Balaji Mandir was built in 1940; the Rath Yatra was suspended after an accident in 1978 and revived in 1991
Rituals: Devotees pull the large rath; tradition states each devotee pulls it for 5–8 steps for blessing
Fair Activities: Large 33-foot-tall rath procession
Cultural Significance: Preserves a long-standing Balaji worship and Rath Yatra tradition in Dhule

Historical Background: Dedicated to the gram devta of Khandesh; preparations begin about 15 days before the festival
Rituals: Married women install the murti; mandap and garbhagriha are decorated; kalash is placed; puja uses 107 types of plants and water from seven rivers; immersion follows
Fair Activities: Music, singing and dancing; grand immersion procession
Cultural Significance: Important Khandesh folk-religious tradition involving family worship, women’s participation, Ahirani songs and community procession

Historical Background: Asthamba is associated with the mythological figure Ashvatthama from the Mahabharata, who is believed by tribal communities to be the son of Guru Dronacharya.
Rituals: N/A
Fair Activities: Annual fair and large tribal gathering
Cultural Significance: The fair is an important tribal gathering connecting the local communities with their religious beliefs and mythological traditions associated with Ashvatthama. It represents the cultural and spiritual traditions of the tribal communities of the Nandurbar region.

Historical Background: The yatra is described as an important cultural event of Nandurbar centered around the worship of Mogi Mata.
Rituals: Puja, processions and community gatherings
Fair Activities: Processions and community gathering
Cultural Significance: The yatra brings nearby communities together through worship, processions and collective participation around Mogi Mata.

Historical Background: The festival has a history of over 350 years and developed from a rural horse fair into a major equestrian and cultural event.
Rituals: Horse parades, exhibitions and other festival programs
Fair Activities: Horse trade, horse exhibitions and sales, horse parades, rural sports, agricultural exhibitions, music, folk performances and entertainment programs
Cultural Significance: Reflects the region’s equestrian heritage and rural cultural traditions while bringing together trade, tradition, agriculture, sports and entertainment.

Historical Background: Traditionally held before the Kharif season; the yatra has developed as both a religious gathering and a major agricultural and cattle market.
Rituals: Worship of gramdevi Kalika Mata
Fair Activities: Bull and agricultural market; purchase and sale of bulls, seeds, spices, farming tools, household goods and bullock carts; folk performances
Cultural Significance: Combines religious devotion with agricultural commerce and rural livelihoods. The cattle market and farming-related trade make it an important economic and cultural gathering in the Khandesh region.

Duration: Preparations begin 15 days in advance; week-long fast before the festival
Historical Background: Historical roots date back to the 13th century during the reign of King Umed Singh; initiated by Rajaphanta and Ganda Thakur to honor their devtas.
Rituals: Communities prepare costumes and musical instruments; observe a week-long fast of celibacy; erect a 40–50-foot bamboo pole; perform puja; transport and erect the pole by hand; Holi fire is lit at dawn.
Fair Activities: Traditional costumes, ghungru, morpies, dholkis, flutes, dances and performances portraying women and wild animals
Cultural Significance: Preserves indigenous traditions, historical customs, traditional music, dance, costumes and community rituals of the Satpura region.

Duration: Annual; between Dhantrayodashi and Lakshmi Pujan
Historical Background: Associated with Ashwatthama of the Mahabharata, who is believed to still appear before devotees in different forms. The pilgrimage has a long-standing connection with the Satpura mountains and Astamba Rishi shrine.
Rituals: Pilgrims undertake a difficult mountain trek through Derani, Jethani, Goryamal, Satghol, Nakatyadeo and Bhimkund before reaching the Astamba Rishi devasthan at over 4,000 feet.
Fair Activities: Mountain pilgrimage; trekking through steep paths, valleys and natural landscapes
Cultural Significance: The yatra connects religious belief, pilgrimage and the natural landscape of the Satpura mountains. It represents a significant spiritual and physically demanding tradition for devotees from the surrounding regions.

Historical Background: The festival is rooted in the culture of the Pawara community and is associated with the folklore of Raja Phanta and Uli-Jugan, a devi also associated in the folklore with a dakin.
Rituals: Bonfire-centered performances; men portray Raja Phanta, Ganda Thakur and Uli; dancers wear traditional headgear and masks.
Fair Activities: Folk dance and dramatic performances around the bonfire; Budhiyo, Bawa, Niskya and Raya performers participate
Cultural Significance: Marks the arrival of spring and preserves Pawara folklore, traditional characters, costumes, masks, dance and community performance traditions.

Historical Background: Described as the Khandeshi ancestor festival and associated with the hottest period of the year.
Rituals: New earthen pots are bought and filled with water; household ancestors are honoured before eating; swings are hung for girls
Fair Activities: Swings for girls
Cultural Significance: Honours household ancestors and emphasizes the use of cool water during the hottest period of the year.

Historical Background: The source describes it as the main annual gathering of Bhil, Pawra and Barela communities across three state lines.
Rituals: Gher dancing moves between villages; marriages are negotiated by mutual choice
Fair Activities: Village-to-village Gher dancing; fairs; marriage negotiations
Cultural Significance: Serves as a major annual gathering for Bhil, Pawra and Barela communities.

Historical Background: Described as a hill fair at the Gorakhnath temple drawing pilgrims from three states.
Rituals: Pilgrimage to Gorakhnath temple
Fair Activities: Hill fair; pilgrimage
Cultural Significance: A major pilgrimage and gathering on the Satpura slope.

Festival Name: Muktabai palkhi and the Ashadhaai wari
Historical Background: Muktabai's palkhi is taken from Muktainagar; dindis walk south to join the Pandharpur wari.
Rituals: Palkhi procession; dindi pilgrimage to Pandharpur
Fair Activities: Palkhi and dindi procession
Cultural Significance: Connects the Ahirani-speaking region with the wider Marathi devotional tradition.

Historical Background: Associated with the old temple cluster at Prakasha.
Rituals: Mass bathing at the Tapi–Gomai confluence
Fair Activities: Fair around the old temple cluster
Cultural Significance: Brings people together for ritual bathing and a fair around the temple area.
